items.title: Agents are sessions, not requests: size GKE node pools for AI agent sessions
items.summary: AI agent sessions remain active and idle for most of the workday, making traditional one-Pod-per-session allocations inefficient for cluster resources. By using open-source tools like Agent Substrate and AX on GKE, developers can park idle sessions in object storage to release compute resources while maintaining session state. This approach optimizes resource utilization and reduces Kubernetes node costs by up to 40%.

items.title: Announcing Long-Context Training on TPUs with MaxText Context Parallelism

Powered by the Tokamax Splash Attention kernel, these strategies effectively manage attention compute and memory bottlenecks without materializing full key-value sequences in high-bandwidth memory. items.title: Agent Distraction
items.summary: Analysis of over 913,000 coding agent sessions reveals that 13% expose agents to inline TODO(b/...) comments. In 6% of encounters, agents act on these comments, with 83% being entirely unprompted by the developer. These detours result in significant overhead—adding 70% more steps, 77% more tokens, and 105% more wait time per session—split between chasing closed tickets (41%) and unauthorized scope creep on open bugs (57%). Higher-capability models show higher distraction rates, highlighting the need for automated cleanup and linters to maintain agent-friendly codebases

items.title: What is Pathways? Single-controller training for large models
items.summary: Pathways is a single-controller distributed training system designed to coordinate large-scale model training across multiple accelerator groups by representing computations as a global dataflow graph. Unlike traditional SPMD models like DDP and FSDP that rely on synchronous collectives, Pathways uses asynchronous dispatch and a central scheduler to maximize hardware utilization and prevent deadlocks in complex workloads. By decoupling model definition from physical hardware via virtual devices, developers can efficiently scale complex training architectures and seamlessly handle dynamic workloads like reinforcement learning post-training.

items.title: My dual-axis chart was lying about zero
items.summary: A commenter on Reddit looked at one of my charts for about ten seconds and found a bug I had shipped to everyone. The chart was a combo chart: revenue as bars on the left axis, profit margin as a line on the right axis. Pretty standard dashboard stuff. Their question was simple: "where is zero on the right axis?" It wasn't where the bars started. Two axes on one chart means two sets of tick labels sharing one set of grid lines. My first version got half of that right. The right axis picked the same number of ticks as the left, each one a round number, so every label sat neatly on a grid line. What it never did was force the two zeros onto the same line. Take revenue from $0 to $62K and a margin between −10% and 35%: Left axis: 0, 20K, 40K, 60K, 80K (five lines) Right axis: five lines, round step, must cover −10% to 35%, so: −20%, 0%, 20%, 40%, 60% Look at the second line. The right axis says 0%, the left says $20K. The bars stand on the bottom line, but the margin's zero floats one line above it. Now give one month a −5% margin. The dot lands above the bars' baseline. items.summary: The homepage of ramrom.io used to open with a feature list. A tidy row of bullets: no sign-up, no watermark, works on every platform, free forever. It read well, it said nothing, and it did not help anyone download a video. I replaced it with three steps, each with a small picture: copy the link, paste it here, download. That was the whole change, and it was the best copy decision I have made on the site so far. A feature list describes the tool. A visitor does not arrive wanting a description; they arrive with a link in their clipboard and one question: how do I get this video onto my phone? Every line of a feature list is an answer to a question nobody asked. "No watermark" is only interesting after you already trust the tool. Worse, the list pushed the actual tool down the page. On a phone, which is where most of my visitors are, the link box was below the fold. items.title: Node.js Express Background Jobs: EdTech API Requests, Queue Workers, Idempotency
items.summary: Short answer: an Express endpoint should record an edtech cleanup request and its outbox event in one Postgres transaction, return 202 Accepted, and let a separate worker publish and consume a small job. The worker should claim work with a lease, make each deletion decision idempotent, and write the audit event before acknowledging the delivery. That arrangement keeps a web request short while making recovery inspectable. The constraint comes first. A student-record cleanup can touch thousands of rows, object references, and retention exceptions; keeping the browser request open turns a normal timeout or deploy into an ambiguous business event. The API is therefore an admission point, not the executor. The queue is delivery machinery, not the system of record. There is no magic exactly-once execution guarantee. The useful guarantee is that repeating a delivery cannot create a second externally visible cleanup, and that an operator can tell the difference between queued, running, retryable, completed, and rejected work. items.title: Shipment Fan-Out: Node.js Background Queue Workers, Ack/Nack, Dead Letters, Idempotency
items.summary: Short answer: to create a Node.js background job queue for shipment updates, give each subscriber a queue delivery, acknowledge only after the update is durably accepted, retry only transient failures, and make the worker idempotent because fan-out delivery is at-least-once in the failure cases that matter. That decision is more important than the queue client. A shipment update may need to reach a carrier portal, a warehouse dashboard, a customer notification service, and an internal audit stream. Those destinations do not share latency, availability, or retry behavior. Treating the fan-out as one large request makes the slowest subscriber define the whole operation; treating it as independent jobs gives each delivery its own attempt history and audit trail. The ledger-minded rule is simple: a message is not complete because a worker received it, and it is not complete because an HTTP call returned. It is complete when the business result and the idempotency record have crossed the same durable boundary. items.title: I load-tested HQ Trivia 2.0 with 1,000,000 bots
items.summary: The code in this post is simplified to show the patterns. It isn't Savvy's production source. 1,000,000 concurrent bots, every hub method under 200 ms. That was the goal, and the final run hit it. A custom bot fleet: SignalR bots that play the real game, 200 per container instance, 5,000 Azure Container Instances for the full million. A realistic join curve: 25% of the bots join in the same moment, the way players do when the "show is live" push notification lands. A Redis remote control: runners wait for a start command, so a fleet that takes 30+ minutes to provision still starts in sync. Word submission went from a 10 s average to under 200 ms: HybridCache for show config, player state in memory, and Redis writes moved to a background queue. items.summary: Server Actions fail in three quiet ways, and none of them throws where the bug actually is. Symptom. Three failures appear after moving a form to Server Actions. The action validates, redirect("/dashboard") runs, the browser stays on the form. Or every upload over a megabyte dies with 413 Request Entity Too Large / Body exceeded 1mb limit. Or useActionState never updates — the action throws, and all the user sees is a generic An error occurred in the Server Components render with a digest instead of your message. Cause. redirect() and notFound() do not return; they throw a framework-controlled exception that unwinds the render. A try/catch around the call swallows it, and the action completes normally. items.summary: Our Mac menu bar app has two buttons, Free Agent RAM and Stop Runaways. Each one runs a small Node.js script that finds agent processes eating memory or CPU, and stops them. When the script finishes, the app shows a receipt that lists what it did. If Node.js isn't installed, the script can't run. The app handles that: it shows "Couldn't free agent memory" and says what went wrong. Before the 1.2.10 release it also did something else first. It ran xcrun simctl shutdown all, which shuts down every simulator on the Mac. The order was the bug. In both button handlers, the call that shuts down simulators sat above the check for whether Node.js had run. A person without Node.js would click the button, see "Nothing was changed", and have every running simulator shut down anyway. The receipt was false. The LLM either replies directly or asks to call a tool (get_menu, create_order, payment_link). Your code runs the tool and sends the result back. This repeats until the model has a final answer. items.title: Your AI agent has too much access
items.summary: Most conversations about agent security start with the model: can it be tricked, can it be jailbroken, can a hidden instruction in a web page or a ticket change its behavior. Those are real questions. But they are the wrong place to put your defenses. Assume the model will, at some point, do something you didn't intend. Then ask the only question you actually control: what can it do when that happens? OWASP's Top 10 for LLM Applications calls it Excessive Agency (LLM06:2025): damaging actions performed in response to unexpected, ambiguous or manipulated model output, whatever caused the model to misbehave. OWASP traces it to three root causes: Excessive functionality: the agent can reach tools it doesn't need. OWASP's example is an extension meant to read documents that can also modify and delete them. Excessive permissions: the tool runs with broader rights than the task needs. A "read" extension that connects to the database with an identity that can also update, insert and delete. Excessive autonomy: high-impact actions go through without a person confirming them. Notice that none of the three is about the model. All three are design decisions in the code around it. The company was already struggling to get its first e-bikes to customers due to a litany of supply chain headaches and the complexity of building a futuristic bike powered almost entirely by software. items.title: We Turned On Row-Level Security in Postgres. Four Things Broke.
items.summary: Row-level security looks like a one-line change in Postgres: create a policy, set a session variable, done. We turned it on for a multi-tenant commerce backend, and it took four fixes before it worked. Here they are, along with the decision we had to make. Every tenant-scoped table has a policy that compares its tenant_id to a session variable, app.tenant_id. The API sets that variable on each connection, from the authenticated user's tenant. A query that forgets its tenant filter gets no rows instead of another tenant's rows. That is the backstop we wanted. EF Core query filters already scope tenant reads for tenant-entity types, but a future handler that forgets the filter should fail closed, not leak. The app connects as a least-privilege role, not the superuser. Migrations run as a separate role. The interceptor resets the role and sets the tenant in a single command text. With a parameter in the same command, Npgsql's extended protocol rejects multiple statements. The fix was two calls instead of one. It is a small change, and it failed on the first real request. items.summary: Five edge cases a quote form has to survive: the back button, validation on step two, the mobile keyboard covering the submit button, a page refresh and the success state. The Multi-step lead form in Facade is the version that survives all five, and this article explains how it is built so you can write your own or install it and understand what you are getting. A single long form has one advantage: everything is visible. On a desktop that is fine. On a phone, a form with eight fields is a wall, and the field that matters most to the business, the phone number, is at the bottom. Splitting the form into three screens changes the psychology. The first screen asks a question the visitor wants to answer: what kind of work do you need? That is not data entry, it is describing their problem. By the time contact details come up, they have invested two steps and the request feels half done. I do not have a study to cite for this; I have the pattern working on client sites and the inbox to show for it. Three steps is the number I settled on. Service, Details, Contact. items.summary: Effort 2 is the step worth taking for WebP in sharp. On a 1920 × 1076 photo at quality 80, effort 0 wrote 130.9 KB in 34 ms. Effort 2 wrote 110.4 KB in 60 ms, which is 15.6% smaller for 26 ms more. Effort 6 wrote 102.3 KB but took 214 ms. The default, effort 4, sits in the middle at 106.9 KB and 141 ms. Here is the script, what it printed, and how the curve changes for screenshots and lossless files. The effort option is CPU effort, from 0 (fastest) to 6 (slowest), with a default of 4. The sharp output docs say that and little more. In plain terms, it sets how many encoding tools the encoder tries before it settles. Effort does not change quality. At a fixed quality, a higher effort should give a smaller file of about the same picture. The next sections test that claim. Decode and resize once, keep the raw pixels, then time only the encode. items.title: Retrieval Architecture for Fresh Multi Tenant SaaS Help Centers Explained
items.summary: The constraint that changes this design is freshness: a help-center answer must not leak a document from another tenant, and it must stop citing an old chunk after an article changes. Short answer: use staged retrieval with explicit collections, bounded queries, and traceable source context. Treat ingestion, querying, and citation as separate observable stages, then prove the contract with a small labeled evaluation set before production. Start with the answer users should see, then work backwards to the retrieval unit. For a media SaaS help center, I use a chunk with tenant_id, document_id, version, locale, and updated_at. A query is bounded by tenant and collection; it never relies on a prompt instruction to enforce privacy. Freshness is a policy: for example, reject a chunk whose version is older than the document version recorded by ingestion. This is the unglamorous part. It is also where most expensive bugs begin. A short labeled set of real questions, expected source documents, and an acceptable freshness window gives you a baseline for recall and citation accuracy. items.title: How an options desk earns the right to trade real money
items.summary: Strikedeck does not let a strategy touch real money until it has completed 50 paper trades at a 45 percent win rate or better, with daily loss caps and a kill switch in front of every order. Only then is the desk promoted from PAPER to LIMITED LIVE, and full LIVE still needs an operator token. Most trading tools treat risk controls as a settings page. The user ticks a box, and the box can be unticked at the worst possible moment. Strikedeck treats the gate as part of the product, not as an option. The desk starts in PAPER. Every signal is logged and filled against live prices, but no order leaves the machine. The desk has to prove itself on the same data it would later trade on. That design says something to the person using it. The software is not asking for trust up front. It asks for 50 trades of evidence first, and it shows the count on screen the whole time. The desk connects to Zerodha Kite and streams ticks, open interest and Greeks over Socket.IO for 24 symbols, NIFTY and BANKNIFTY among them. The option chain, the put-call ratio and max pain update as the market moves. Nothing in that stream places an order on its own. Three engines look at the same market state and vote.

items.summary: Agent Monitor: native desktop widgets for Claude Code and Codex. Usage limits at a glance, plus a live list of sessions stuck on approvals, questions or your next prompt. My usual afternoon looks like this: three or four Claude Code and Codex sessions running in parallel, in different projects, in different windows. One is refactoring an API, one is writing tests, one is fixing a landing page. And every twenty minutes I discover that one of them has been sitting there for a quarter of an hour, politely waiting for me to approve npm run deploy. Another one asked me a question and went idle. A third finished ages ago and I never noticed. The agents got fast. I became the bottleneck. So I built a small thing to fix that. Agent Monitor is a native macOS app with WidgetKit widgets and a menu bar icon. It answers two questions without me opening anything: Who is waiting on me, and why? A versão segue o modelo de suporte padrão (Standard Term Support, STS) e terá dois anos de manutenção; o .NET 10 permanece como opção de suporte de longo prazo. O lançamento coincidiu com a .NET Conf, realizada de 10 a 13 de novembro de 2026. No primeiro dia do evento, 10 de novembro, .NET 8 e .NET 9 chegaram ao fim do suporte. A mudança exige que equipes com aplicações nessas versões avaliem as opções de atualização disponíveis. C# 15 é a versão padrão para projetos direcionados ao .NET 11. A linguagem adiciona tipos de união, declarados com a palavra-chave union, e o compilador verifica se expressões switch cobrem todas as possibilidades desses tipos. Hierarquias fechadas limitam a derivação ao assembly que as declara. items.title: Understanding Redux Toolkit in React.js – A Beginner-Friendly Guide
items.summary: When building React applications, we usually manage data using useState. This works well for small applications. But imagine an application with multiple components that need to access and update the same data. For example, in a Task Management Application: One component adds a task. Another component displays the tasks. Another component deletes a task. Another component updates a task. Managing the same data across multiple components can become difficult. Redux is a JavaScript library used for managing application state globally. In simple words, Redux provides a central place to store application data so that different components can access and update it. Instead of passing data from one component to another using props, components can directly access the required data from the Redux store. Redux Toolkit (RTK) is the official recommended way to write Redux logic. Earlier, developers had to write more code to configure Redux, create actions, and manage reducers. Redux Toolkit simplifies this process by providing ready-to-use functions. Some important benefits: Less boilerplate code. Easier state management. Helps avoid common Redux mistakes. items.title: Don't Hold a Database Transaction While the LLM Thinks
items.summary: Every call to a language model costs money. If your users pay with prepaid credits, each call is charged against a balance that other calls are spending at the same moment. I built this on top of my PostgreSQL double-entry wallet ledger, and both obvious designs turned out to be wrong. Charge inside one transaction. Open a transaction, lock the balance row, call the model, write the charge, commit. This never overspends, but the row lock is held for as long as the model takes to answer: seconds, sometimes much longer. Every other operation on that wallet waits behind it, including a top-up or a second AI call, and a pooled connection sits idle the whole time. Charge after the call. Call the model first, then write the charge. Nothing is locked while the model runs, but nothing is reserved either. Twenty requests can read the same balance, all call the model, and all try to charge. Without a constraint, the balance goes negative. With a non-negative constraint, the late charges fail, which is no better: the model has already done the work, and you can't bill for it. The fix is the one card payments use: an authorization hold. items.summary: Aynı müşteriden aynı anda iki istek geldi. İkisi de bizim bakiye kontrolümüzden geçti. Biri bankaya gitti ve "bakiye yetersiz" diye geri döndü. Müşteri ekranda bir hata mesajı gördü ve şikâyet etti. Biz sorunu o şikâyetten öğrendik. Kodda bariz bir hata yoktu. Bakiyeyi okuyor, yetip yetmediğine bakıyor, sonra düşüyorduk. Tek başına çalışan bir istek için bu doğru. Sorun, aynı hesap için iki isteğin aynı anda çalışmasıydı. Kısa cevap: bakiyeyi önce okuyup sonra ayrı bir komutla düşme. Kontrolü ve düşümü tek bir atomik veritabanı işlemine koy. Bunun üç yolu var: okurken satırı kilitlemek (UPDLOCK, PostgreSQL'de FOR UPDATE), kontrolü UPDATE'in WHERE koşuluna taşımak ya da satırın sürümünü (rowversion) kontrol etmek. Transaction'a sarmak tek başına yetmez. Bu hatanın adı race condition: sonuç, iki işlemin hangi sırayla çalıştığına bağlı. Bakiyede aldığı şekle check-then-act deniyor. items.title: Webhook nedir, gelmezse ne yapmalı?
items.summary: Bir gün raporda bir ödemenin satırı eksik kaldı. Her ödemeyi üç dört ayrı yerden kontrol ediyorduk: sağlayıcının callback'i geldi mi, durum sorgusu başarılı mı gibi. O ödemede diğer işaretler tamamdı. Yalnızca callback işaretlenmemişti. Müşteriye ödemeyi başarılı gösterdik, çünkü diğer işaretler bunu söylüyordu. Ama callback'in neden gelmediğini sağlayıcıya sorduk. Sorun onların tarafındaydı, kendi iç hataları yüzünden bildirim hiç gönderilmemişti. Bizim tarafta hata yoktu. I'm a solo indie developer, and yesterday I submitted a new build of Fambind, my family organization app for iOS, with a layout optimized for the foldable iPhone. It's in App Review now. A new screen shape is a rare chance to look good while most apps still look stretched or awkward. For a small indie app, being ready early is one of the few advantages I have over bigger teams. It also forced me to clean up assumptions I had been carrying around for years. No more hardcoded sizes. Anything that assumed "an iPhone is this wide" had to go. Adaptive layouts. Screens adjust to the space they get instead of assuming one fixed shape. Using the extra room well. On a bigger canvas, a family app can show more at once, like a shared calendar next to the details, without more taps. Testing in the simulator at different sizes, including the ones I hope are close to the real thing. If your layout only works on one screen size, you have a bug you haven't found yet. items.title: SQL Server migration verification: matching row counts are only the start
items.summary: After a SQL Server migration, matching row counts are a useful first check. They tell you that two tables contain the same number of rows. They do not tell you whether those rows contain the same values, or whether the destination contains the same primary keys. One missing row and one extra row can leave the total unchanged. Smaller differences can also survive a count check: an accent removed from a name, a decimal changed from 12.50 to 12.51, or a NULL converted to empty text. The row still exists, but its content has changed. A useful acceptance report needs to distinguish missing rows, extra rows, and rows whose values differ under the same key. The verifier described here is a small .NET 8 command-line tool for comparing selected tables between two SQL Server databases. It reads COUNT_BIG(*) and asks SQL Server to calculate a SHA-256 hash for each row. Rows are matched using their complete primary keys, including composite keys. The primary key identifies the row; the row hash represents its serialized column values. The implementation retains full serialized key bytes rather than reducing primary keys to hashes. A changed primary-key value therefore appears as a missing row

items.title: Inside swiftc: How Swift Turns Source into SIL, LLVM IR and Machine Code
items.summary: One small function followed through every stage of the Swift compiler, with real SIL, LLVM IR and x86-64 / ARM64 assembly, and a measured look at how optimization changes the cost of protocols, generics, closures and classes. Source → Lexer → Parser → AST → Type checker → SIL → SIL optimizer → LLVM IR → LLVM optimizer → Machine code → Object file → Linker → Binary Last year I lost most of an afternoon to a single line of arithmetic. It was in a geometry helper, nothing clever, a handful of numbers, a couple of Double(...) conversions and some parentheses. Every clean build took noticeably longer than it should have, and when I finally ran the compiler with type-checking timers switched on, that one line was the culprit. That sent me down a path I'd been avoiding for years: actually reading what swiftc produces between my source file and the binary. This article is the write-up I wish I'd had at the start. We'll follow one tiny function through every stage of the pipeline. We'll look at real SIL, real LLVM IR and real assembly. items.title: I shipped a habit app that only allows one habit
items.summary: Most habit apps become a second todo list. You add ten habits on day one, miss half of them on day two, and stop opening the app by day four. I shipped an iPhone app, bububaba, that refuses that loop. You start with one daily habit. Finish it, earn one water drop, and water a tree. The tree grows from sprout to sapling to mature, then you harvest fruit. Leave it too long and it wilts. A run of finished days brings it back. A second habit stays locked until you complete 30 days in a row. The app is free, English and Vietnamese, iOS 17 or later: bububaba on the App Store. I did not limit the app to one habit because the data model was hard. A list of habits is the easy version. The limit is there so the home screen can answer a single question: did I do the thing today? A Home Screen widget shows the task that is still waiting. The reminder fires at the time you choose, again near the end of the day, and when the tree is thirsty. Check-in is a tap, with an optional note and photo. That is the whole daily path. The 30-day lock is the part I would keep if I rewrote it. Adding a new habit feels like progress. It is usually a way to abandon the one you already picked. The lock makes that

items.summary: An anonymous reader quotes a report from The Hill: The Pan American Health Organization (PAHO) confirmed Tuesday that it was withdrawing the U.S.'s measles elimination status, ending more than two decades of what is considered to be one of the greatest public health achievements in modern history. The U.S. met with PAHO's Measles and Rubella Elimination Regional Monitoring and Re-Verification Commission for a three-day, closed-door meeting last week. "The commission concluded that the endemic measles transmission has now been reestablished in Bolivia, Mexico and the United States, and recommended that their measles elimination status be withdrawn, a recommendation which I have accepted," Jarbas Barbosa, PAHO's director, said during the briefing Tuesday. The U.S. achieved measles elimination status in 2000 and has held onto that for more than 25 years. But the past two years have seen close to 8,000 measles infections and roughly a dozen related deaths. This year has been the worst in terms of transmission in more than 30 years. The Associated Press reports: The embattled company's board of directors "unanimously accepted his resignation and does not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO," Nvidia Chairman Harvey Jones said at the start of Nvidia's quarterly earnings call before yielding to Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress, who is running the company as a permanent replacement is sought. [...] Earlier on Tuesday, Huang said in a social media post that if the board decided that his return was in the best interest of shareholders, employees, the company and the country, he would be "honored to answer these calls." He acknowledged making "serious mistakes" in his personal life. items.summary: By the time someone asks who changed the amount on this record last month, it is usually months later. Whoever is asking has neither the screen as it looked then nor the build that was running, only the few rows left behind at the time. Who logged in, who changed which field from what to what, who looked at which record: every decision in the auditing layer has to assume that scene first, including the ones that look like nothing more than saving space. We've also taken steps to secure affected user accounts and put additional protections in place to prevent unauthorized code from being delivered." items.title: School Phone Bans Are Gradually Improving Test Scores
items.summary: An anonymous reader quotes a report from The New York Times: School cellphone bans are beginning to modestly improve students' academic performance, according to the first large national analysis that compared students' test scores before and after the bans. Schools with strict bans -- requiring students to lock their phones in pouches all school day -- saw math and reading scores improve as if students had an additional week or two of school a year, the study found. It was published Tuesday by the Center for Education Policy Research at Harvard. U.S. students' test scores began falling over a decade ago. The drop coincided with the rise of smartphones, raising questions about their role in the decline. The evidence so far on the academic effects of phone bans has been mixed. But the new study indicates they are starting to have an influence. The study looked at 3.3 million students between 2021 and 2026. They were in third through 10th grade, attending 4,600 U.S. schools. Using scores on MAP tests, which track achievement from fall to spring, it compared the performance of students at schools that put in strict phone bans with those at similar schools that did not have such bans.

items.title: BugMeNot Calls It Quits
items.summary: BugMeNot, the password-sharing service launched in 2003 to help users bypass website registration requirements, has shut down without explanation after more than two decades. All that's left on the website is a farewell message that reads: "Thanks to everyone who envisioned a better internet." heise online reports: Founded by Guy King, the service had been online since 2003: BugMeNot was a collection of login credentials for various online services. Volunteers submitted credentials they had created for different websites. The idea was simple: Nobody wants to create a full account and provide all their sensitive information just to use a service occasionally. Two decades ago, this privacy concern was more firmly embedded in the public consciousness, but it has since faded considerably. Back then, usernames and passwords were usually the only access controls, so people could easily submit those credentials. Multifactor authentication was still exotic, and passkeys were a distant prospect. The once-popular service lost its shine after just a few years. items.title: Muting the mic for every app on macOS with Core Audio
items.summary: Zoom, Teams and Meet each have their own mute, and they don't know about each other. I wanted one hotkey that mutes the mic for everything, so I made a small menu bar app for it. It sets kAudioDevicePropertyMute on the input devices through Core Audio, so every app just gets silence. By default it mutes all inputs, not only the default one, because Zoom and Meet often disagree about which mic is "the" mic. It also listens for changes and puts the mute back if some app flips it. ⌘⇧M toggles it, and there's push to talk too. Later I added optional local recording of the mic plus system audio into one small file, which is handy for dropping a call into ChatGPT or Claude for a summary. It's free and MIT, macOS 14+: github.com/oochernyshev/lockmic. I'm the developer, happy to answer Core Audio questions.

items.title: How to check a license key in your Mac app offline
items.summary: Short answer: Sign each license on your server with Ed25519, then verify it in the app with CryptoKit and the matching public key. Honest customers stay unlocked offline, because the check does not need a network call. Verify the signature and the expiry at launch and again where the paid feature runs, not in a single isLicensed() flag. A shared serial list, or a secret compiled into the app, can be copied out of the binary. Anyone who has that secret can invent keys your app will accept, or share one serial widely. AI tools make that read faster than it used to be. A signed license works the other way around. Your server holds a private key and signs a small payload: the customer's email, the product name, and an expiry. The app ships the public key and uses it to verify the signature. The public key cannot issue a new license. Sign the raw payload bytes. Then ship the payload and the signature as standard Base64, joined by a period: base64(payload) + "." + base64(signature) The payload is JSON, for example: {"email":"customer@example.com","product":"MyApp","expiry":"2027-11-17T00:00:00Z"} Leave the payload machine-agnostic unless you have a clear reason to bind a device, so the s

items.summary: Wakaru is a menu bar app that turns any audio playing on your Mac into translated subtitles, fully on-device. In version 1.1.2, I fixed two issues: "right?" getting translated as the direction "right", and the last word of a sentence popping up again as its own caption. Short questions and tag questions such as "right?" were translated with the wrong meaning Right after a sentence was shown, its last word sometimes came back as a caption of its own In English meetings people end sentences with "right?" or "you know what?" all the time. If you are following a conversation through subtitles, that is the kind of thing that makes you lose the thread for a second. items.title: How InkHammy checks grammar in every Mac app with the Accessibility API
items.summary: I'm Zak, and I build InkHammy, a grammar checker that runs as a Mac menu bar app and as an iPhone keyboard. Disclosure up front: InkHammy is my product. This post isn't a review; it's a write-up of how the Mac app reads and fixes text inside other apps through the macOS Accessibility API, and the design choices that came out of it. A browser extension only sees web pages. A lot of writing on a Mac happens somewhere else: Slack, Mail, Notes, Messages, the ChatGPT app, and text fields inside desktop apps built on web views. To check text in all of them, an app has to follow whichever field has focus, read its text, know where each word sits on screen, and write corrections back without breaking the host app. macOS exposes this through the Accessibility API (AX). The user grants Accessibility permission once in System Settings, and the app can then observe and act on UI elements in other processes. AX is powerful, but every host app implements it a little differently, and a call into a busy app can block. Most of InkHammy's Mac architecture exists to deal with those two facts. items.title: Why I took Whisper out of my iPhone transcription app before it shipped
items.summary: I work on Koedori at W Lab. It is an iPhone app that records a lecture, a meeting or an interview and turns it into text on the phone itself, with no account, and the audio is never uploaded. The early builds ran Whisper through WhisperKit. The version on the App Store has no Whisper in it at all: it uses Apple's SpeechAnalyzer framework and its SpeechTranscriber module. This post is about why, and what building on SpeechTranscriber is like. Koedori makes three promises: transcription is free and needs no account, audio never leaves the phone, and re-transcribing costs nothing, as often as you like. The second one is architecture, not a setting. There is no code path that uploads audio, and the app has no server of its own. So recognition has to run on the device, and it has to be cheap enough to run again on a whim. Whisper on the phone met that on paper. The trouble was everything around the model. WhisperKit compiles a model for the Neural Engine the first time it loads it. On the iPhone 14 I measured, the first load of large-v3 turbo after an install took 197 to 205 seconds, every time. A reload within the same install took 4 seconds, and a 10-second clip then transcribed in 0.

items.title: Eliminating Nondeterminism in LLM Inference with Integer-Only Arithmetic (15 minute read)
items.summary: A floating-point number stores a fixed number of significant digits and a separate exponent. When two numbers with very different exponents are added, the small one has to be shifted to line up with the big one, and the digits that fall off on the end are gone. That means that (a+b)+c is not always equal to a+(b+c). This post looks at what happens when integer addition, which is exact, is used.

items.title: Handing over humanity (22 minute read)
items.summary: Some AI experts believe that once we achieve superintelligence, humans will be permanently disempowered, and we shall all be ruled by an AI god. This might not be such a desirable outcome, as humans have a natural desire for freedom. The arrangement will probably not work, as keeping power responsive to human needs has required checks developed over centuries, sustained by repeated feedback from the real world and correction, and there's no reason to keep that equilibrium stable once humans have surrendered all control. Humans have the ability now to steer the technology in a way that will not lead to a complete replacement of human judgment.

items.title: LLMs can learn some multi-step reasoning on filler tokens instead of visible CoT (9 minute read)
items.summary: By changing the training setup and applying LoRAs to Qwen3.6-35B-A3B and gpt-oss-20b, researchers taught models to do some multi-step tasks while emitting only filler tokens, beating an answer-only baseline on three of seven tasks. They also mapped theoretical layer-depth limits and showed empirical walls, with some tasks learned out to 60 steps and others failing after one to three. The work is meant to separate filler-token reasoning from steganographic hidden reasoning when interpreting chain-of-thought.

items.title: What objective is reasoning solving? (12 minute read)
items.summary: Reasoning is pathfinding in token space. There are many paths from the problem to a correct answer, and the model traverses each of them with each sample. A path is not guaranteed to converge to the correct answer - it's only in aggregate, over the distribution of paths, do we get a high probability of success. RL training directly raises the success probability. The gains credited to 'thinking longer' come from the search paid for during training rather than at inference.

items.title: Two Kinds of Test-Time Scaling (28 minute read)
items.summary: Test-time scaling trades compute for performance at test time. There are two types of test-time scaling: one allows researchers to trade more compute for more performance per task, but only up to the maximum quantity of per-task compute used during training; and the other lets researchers trade more compute for more performance per task, and lets them do so up to quantities of compute and performance that never occurred during training. Scaling methods that permit the latter change will have a larger impact than test-time scaling considered simply. This essay describes how this may impact the world.

items.title: They Created a Cell That's Almost Alive. What to Do With It Now? (8 minute read)
items.summary: A SpudCell is an artificial cell created from lifeless ingredients that can grow, copy its DNA, divide in two, and start its cell cycle all over again. It is still far from a self-sustaining cell that any scientist could manufacture from prepared ingredients, but the technology could eventually make it easier to produce medicines, foods, and other items that could not otherwise be produced with ordinary biology. The researchers working on SpudCell hope that it will eventually be a platform for biotechnology that will allow a simple cell to be engineered in scores of useful ways. SpudCell could potentially be misused, so its researchers are taking security seriously from the start - its DNA and proteins are engineered so that it can only survive on an exotic diet of chemicals not found in nature.
